props.title: From the ad to the conversion in four steps
props.subtitle: One direction, no detours. No menu to wander into, no form to fill, no second offer: the visitor either understands and clicks, or scrolls to understand more and then clicks.

items.title: The campaign makes a promise
items.description: An ad, a post or an email says one thing. Visitors arrive with that sentence in their head, so the first screen says the same thing, louder.

items.title: The bridge explains and reassures
items.description: A checkout shows a price; a store listing shows screenshots. Neither explains why. The bridge does: benefit, preview, proof, in two or three screens at most.

items.title: The visitor clicks through
items.description: To the checkout, the signup or the store, already knowing what they will find there.

items.title: The destination converts
items.description: It only has to confirm what the bridge made clear. Fewer abandoned carts and signups, because the objections were handled one page earlier.

props.title: What a click-through page needs to carry
props.subtitle: Six things, in roughly this order. Skip the ones your destination already does well.

items.title: Message match
items.description: The headline uses the words of the ad or email that brought the visitor. Different words feel like a wrong turn.

items.title: The benefit before the mechanics
items.description: What changes for the visitor, then how it works. The destination will handle the details.

items.title: A preview of the other side
items.description: Show what happens after the click: a screenshot, the steps, the time it takes. Surprises kill conversions.

items.title: Proof, briefly
items.description: One or two real quotes or figures. The bridge is short; save the case studies for the destination.

items.title: One destination, repeated
items.description: Every button goes to the same URL with the same label. Three placements: hero, after proof, end.

items.title: Nothing else
items.description: No newsletter box, no footer maze, no chat popup. Anything that is not the click is friction.

props.title: What stays on the bridge, and what waits on the other side
props.subtitle: The most reusable table on the page: whatever sits in the right-hand column belongs on the destination, so delete it from the bridge.

props.title: Questions people ask before they click
props.subtitle: Short answers: a bridge page should not become a sales page. The same answers feed a FAQ rich result in search.

items.title: What is a click-through landing page?
items.description: A page between a campaign and the place where the conversion happens (a checkout, a signup, an app store listing). It has no form of its own; its job is to explain the offer and make the next click an easy decision.

items.title: When is a click-through page better than sending traffic straight to the offer?
items.description: When the destination is cold: a checkout that shows a price before explaining value, a signup that asks for a card, a store listing with no room for context. The bridge page supplies the missing context first.

items.title: How many buttons should it have, and where should they go?
items.description: As many as you like, as long as they all go to the same place with the same wording. One in the hero, one after the proof and one at the end cover visitors who decide early, in the middle and late.

items.title: Should the button open the destination in a new tab?
items.description: Usually not. A click-through page hands the visitor over; opening a new tab leaves the bridge behind them and splits attention.

items.title: How do I measure whether it works?
items.description: Track the click-through rate to the destination, and the conversion rate on the destination for visitors who came through the bridge versus those who did not. If the second number does not improve, the bridge is not adding context, only a step.

items.title: How do I adapt this page with AstroWind?
items.description: Point every button at your destination, replace the copy in each widget and keep the order. Every block is a reusable widget; no custom code is involved.
